readings.c1s1:
¶
'''bewet'''<sup>1</sup> (bẹ̄-wet′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bewetted'', ''bewet'', ppr. ''bewetting''. [< ME. ''beweten'', < ''be-'' + ''weten'', wet: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wet''.] To wet; moisten.
{{smaller block|His napkin with his true tears all ''bewet''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1.}}}}

'''bewet'''<sup>2</sup>, '''bewit''' (bū′et, -it), ''n.'' [< late ME. ''bewette'', dim. of OF. ''beue'', ''bue'', earlier ''buie'', ''boie'', a collar, chain, fetter, < L. ''boiæ'', a collar for the neck, whence also ult. E. ''buoy'', q. v.] In ''falconry'', the leather with which the bell was attached to a hawk’s leg. [Commonly in the plural.]

'''bewhisper''' (bẹ̄-hwis′pėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''whisper''.] To whisper. ''Fairfax.'' [Rare.]

'''bewhore†''' (bẹ̄-hōr′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''whore''.] '''1.''' To make a whore of. ''Beau. and Fl.''—'''2.''' To call or pronounce a whore. ''Shak.''

'''bewield''' (bẹ̄-wēld′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''bewelden'', < ''be-'' + ''welden'', wield: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wield''.] To wield, handle, or control; manage. ''J. Harrison.'' [Rare.]

'''bewigged''' (bẹ̄-wigd′), ''p. a.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wigged''.] Wearing a wig.
{{smaller block|Ancient ladies and ''bewigged'' gentlemen seemed hurrying to enjoy a social cup of tea.
{{right|''L. M. Alcott'', Hospital Sketches, p. 20.}}}}

'''bewilder''' (bẹ̄-wil′dėr), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wilder'': see ''wilder''.] '''1.''' To confuse as to direction or situation; cause to lose the proper road or course: as, the intricacy of the streets ''bewildered'' him; to be ''bewildered'' in the woods.
{{smaller block|<poem>Can this be the bird, to man so good,
That, after their ''bewildering'',
Covered with leaves the little children,</poem>}}
readings.c2s3:
<poem>{{smaller block|Like slaves you sold your souls for golden dross,
''Bewraying'' her to death.
{{right|''Massinger'', Virgin-Martyr, ii. 3.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|Hide the outcast, ''bewray'' not him that wandereth, is the simplest lesson of common humanity.
{{right|''W. Phillips'', Speeches, p. 97.}}}}
'''4.''' To reveal or disclose unintentionally or incidentally; show the presence or true character of; show or make visible.
{{smaller block|The ointment of his right hand which ''bewrayeth'' itself.
{{right|Prov. xxvii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy speech ''bewrayeth'' thee.
{{right|Mat. xxvi. 73.}}}}
[''Bewray'' is still sometimes used, especially in poetry, as an archaic word.]

'''bewrayer†''' (bẹ̄-rā′ėr), ''n.'' A betrayer or divulger.
{{smaller block|A ''bewrayer'' of secrets.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 225.}}}}

'''bewrayingly†''' (bẹ̄-rā′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a manner to bewray.

'''bewrayment†''' (bẹ̄-rā′mẹnt), ''n.'' [< ''bewray'' + ''-ment.''] The act of bewraying.

'''bewreak†''' (bẹ̄-rēk′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''bewreken'', < ''be-'' + ''wreken'', wreak. Cf. AS. ''bewrecan'', exile, send forth: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wreak.''] To avenge; revenge.
{{smaller block|Thus much am I ''bewreke.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale (ed. Speght), l. 809.}}}}

'''bewreck†''' (bẹ̄-rek′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wreck.'' Cf. AS. ''bewrecan'', drive or bring to, of ships: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wreck.''] To ruin; destroy.
{{smaller block|Yet was I, or I parted thence, ''bewreckt.'' ''Mir. for Mags.''}}

'''bewrought†''' (bẹ̄-rôt′). Obsolete past participle of ''bework.''

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bewet|540|beyond}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bewet'''<sup>1</sup> (bẹ̄-wet′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bewetted'', ''bewet'', ppr. ''bewetting''.   [< ME. ''beweten'', < ''be-'' + ''weten'', wet: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wet''.]   To wet; moisten.
{{smaller block|His napkin with his true tears all ''bewet''.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1.}}}}

'''bewet'''<sup>2</sup>, '''bewit''' (bū′et, -it), ''n.''   [< late ME. ''bewette'', dim. of OF. ''beue'', ''bue'', earlier ''buie'', ''boie'', a collar, chain, fetter, < L. ''boiæ'', a collar for the neck, whence also ult. E. ''buoy'', q. v.]   In ''falconry'', the leather with which the bell was attached to a hawk’s leg. [Commonly in the plural.]

'''bewhisper''' (bẹ̄-hwis′pėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''whisper''.]   To whisper.   ''Fairfax.'' [Rare.]

'''bewhore†''' (bẹ̄-hōr′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''whore''.]   '''1.''' To make a whore of.   ''Beau. and Fl.''—'''2.''' To call or pronounce a whore.   ''Shak.''

'''bewield''' (bẹ̄-wēld′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewelden'', < ''be-'' + ''welden'', wield: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wield''.]   To wield, handle, or control; manage.   ''J. Harrison.'' [Rare.]

'''bewigged''' (bẹ̄-wigd′), ''p. a.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wigged''.]   Wearing a wig.
{{smaller block|Ancient ladies and ''bewigged'' gentlemen seemed hurrying to enjoy a social cup of tea.
{{right|''L. M. Alcott'', Hospital Sketches, p. 20.}}}}

'''bewilder''' (bẹ̄-wil′dėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wilder'': see ''wilder''.]   '''1.''' To confuse as to direction or situation; cause to lose the proper road or course: as, the intricacy of the streets ''bewildered'' him; to be ''bewildered'' in the woods.
{{smaller block|<poem>Can this be the bird, to man so good,
That, after their ''bewildering'',
Covered with leaves the little children, So painfully in the wood?</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Redbreast Chasing the Butterfly.}}}}
'''2.''' To lead into perplexity or confusion; perplex; puzzle; confuse.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Bewildering'' odors floating, dulled her sense,
And killed her fear.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 259.}}}}
{{smaller block|We have elementary disturbances of consciousness in diseases of the mind, such as epileptic states, ecstacy, . . . and the ''bewildered'' state of the mind in paralytic dementia. {{right|''E. C. Mann'', Psychol. Med., p. 35.}}}}
='''Syn.''' {{smaller|To confound, confuse, mystify, nonplus.}}

'''bewilderedness''' (bē-wil′dėrd-nes), ''n.'' The state of being bewildered; bewilderment.

'''bewilderingly''' (bē-wil′dėr-ing-li), ''adv.'' In a bewildering manner; so as to bewilder.

'''bewilderment''' (bē-wil′dėr-ment), ''n.''   [< ''bewilder'' + ''-ment''.]   The state of being bewildered.
{{smaller block|Thought was arrested by utter ''bewilderment.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Silas Marner, ii.}}}}

'''bewimple''' (bē-wim′pl), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewimplen'' (= D. ''bewimpelen''), < ''be-'' + ''wimpelen'', wimple: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wimple''.]   To cover with a wimple; veil.   ''Gower.''

'''bewinter''' (bē-win′tėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''winter''.]   To make like winter.
{{smaller block|<poem>Tears that ''bewinter'' all my year.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', Sleep.}}}}

'''bewit''', ''n.'' See ''bewet''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bewitch''' (bē-wich′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewicchen'', ''biwicchen'', < ''be-'' + ''wicchen'', witch: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''witch'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' To subject to the influence of witchcraft; affect by witchcraft or sorcery; throw a charm or spell over.
{{smaller block|<poem>Look how I am ''bewitch’d''; behold, mine arm</poem> Is, like a blasted sapling, wither’d up.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To charm; fascinate; please to such a degree as to take away the power of resistance.
{{smaller block|Love doth ''bewitch'' and strangely change us.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., p. 468.}}}}
{{smaller block|The charms of poetry our souls ''bewitch''.
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires.}}}}
{{smaller block|His [Tennyson’s] verses still ''bewitch'' youths and artists by their sentiments and beauty, but their thought takes hold of thinkers and men of the world.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 160.}}}}

'''bewitchedness''' (bē-wicht′nes), ''n.''   [< ''bewitched'', pp. of ''bewitch'', + ''-ness''.]   The state of being bewitched.

'''bewitcher''' (bẹ̄-wich′ėr), ''n.'' One who bewitches or fascinates.

'''bewitchery''' (bẹ̄-wich′ėr-i), ''n.''   [< ''bewitch'', in imitation of ''witchery''.]   Witchery; fascination; charm. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|There is a certain ''bewitchery'' or fascination in words.
{{right|''South'', Works, II. ix.}}}}

'''bewitchful''' (bẹ̄-wich′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''bewitch'' + ''-ful'' (irregularly suffixed to a verb).]   Alluring; fascinating. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Ill, more ''bewitchful'' to entice away. {{right|''Milton'', Letters.}}}}

'''bewitching''' (bẹ̄-wich′ing), ''a.''   [Ppr. of ''bewitch''.]   Having power to bewitch or fascinate; fascinating; charming: as, “''bewitching'' tenderness,” ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 223.

{{smaller block|The more he considered it, the more ''bewitching'' the scene appeared to him.{{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ii. 5.}}}}

'''bewitchingly''' (bē-wich′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a bewitching manner.

'''bewitchingness''' (bē-wich′ing-nes), ''n.'' The quality which makes a person or thing bewitching.

'''bewitchment''' (bē-wich′ment), ''n.''   [< ''bewitch'' + ''-ment.'']   Fascination; power of charming; the effects of witchcraft.
{{smaller block|I will counterfeit the ''bewitchment'' of some popular man, and give it bountifully to the desirers.{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|To wash in May dew guards against ''bewitchment.''{{right|''Keary'', Prim. Belief, p. 378.}}}}

'''bewith''' (bē′wiᴛ̵ʜ), ''n.''   [< ''be''<sup>1</sup> + ''with''<sup>1</sup>: what one can ''be with'' or do with.]   A makeshift; a substitute. [Scotch.]

'''bewonder''' (bē-wun′dėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wonder;'' = D. ''bewonderen'' = G. ''bewundern'', admire.]   '''1.''' To fill with wonder; amaze.
{{smaller block|<poem>Seeing his astonishment,
How he ''bewondered'' was.</poem>{{right|''Fairfax'', tr. of Tasso, x. 17.}}}}
'''2.''' To wonder at; admire.

'''bework†''' (bē-wėrk′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewurchen'', < AS. ''bewyrcan'' (= D. ''bewerken'' = G. ''bewirken'' = Dan. ''bevirke''), work, work in, adorn, < ''be-'' + ''wyrcan'', work: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''work.'']   To work, as with thread; embroider.
{{smaller block|<poem>The mantelle and the gyrdylle both
That rychely was ''bewroght.''</poem>{{right|''Sir Eglamour'', l. 1152.}}}}
{{smaller block|Smocks all ''bewrought.''{{right|''B. Jonson'', Masque of Owls.}}}}

'''bewpers''', ''n.'' See ''beaupers.''

'''bewrap''' (bē-rap′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bewrapped'', ''bewrapt'', ppr. ''bewrapping''.   [< ME. ''bewrappen'', also ''bewrabben'' (with var. ''bewlappen''), < ''be-'' + ''wrappen'', wrap: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wrap''.]   To wrap up; clothe; envelop.
{{smaller block|<poem>His sword, . . .
''Bewrapt'' with flowers, hung idlie by his side.</poem>
{{right|''Fairfax'', tr. of Tasso, xvi. 30.}}}}

'''bewray†''' (bē-rā′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewraien'', ''biwreyen'', disclose, reveal (= OFries. ''biwrōgia'' = OHG. ''biruogan'', MHG. ''berügen''), < ''be-'' + ''wraien'', ''wreyen'', obs. E. ''wray'', disclose, reveal, < AS. ''wrēgan'', accuse (= OFries. ''wrōgia'', ''wreia'' = OS. ''wrōgian'' = D. ''wroegen'', accuse, = OHG. ''ruogen'', MHG. ''ruegen'', G. ''rügen'', censure, = Icel. ''rægja'', slander, = Sw. ''röja'', betray, = Goth. ''wrōhjan'', accuse), from a noun repr. by Goth. ''wrōhs'', an accusation, = Icel. ''rōg'', a slander. Somewhat affected in sense by ''betray'', a quite different word.]   '''1.''' To accuse; malign.—'''2.''' To reveal; divulge; make known; declare.
{{smaller block|<poem>Write down thy mind, ''bewray'' thy meaning.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing and ''bewrayeth'' it not. Prov. xxix. 24.}}
'''3.''' To disclose or reveal (the identity or the secrets of a person) perfidiously or prejudicially; betray; expose.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou ''bewreiest'' alle secrenesse.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Man of Law’s Tale, l. 675.}}}}
{{smaller block|For feare to be enforced by torments to ''bewray'' his confederates.
{{right|''Knolles'', Hist. Turks, p. 7. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
<poem>{{smaller block|Like slaves you sold your souls for golden dross,
''Bewraying'' her to death.
{{right|''Massinger'', Virgin-Martyr, ii. 3.}}}}</poem>
{{smaller block|Hide the outcast, ''bewray'' not him that wandereth, is the simplest lesson of common humanity.
{{right|''W. Phillips'', Speeches, p. 97.}}}}
'''4.''' To reveal or disclose unintentionally or incidentally; show the presence or true character of; show or make visible.
{{smaller block|The ointment of his right hand which ''bewrayeth'' itself.
{{right|Prov. xxvii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thy speech ''bewrayeth'' thee.
{{right|Mat. xxvi. 73.}}}}
[''Bewray'' is still sometimes used, especially in poetry, as an archaic word.]

'''bewrayer†''' (bẹ̄-rā′ėr), ''n.'' A betrayer or divulger.
{{smaller block|A ''bewrayer'' of secrets.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 225.}}}}

'''bewrayingly†''' (bẹ̄-rā′ing-li), ''adv.'' In a manner to bewray.

'''bewrayment†''' (bẹ̄-rā′mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''bewray'' + ''-ment.'']   The act of bewraying.

'''bewreak†''' (bẹ̄-rēk′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bewreken'', < ''be-'' + ''wreken'', wreak. Cf. AS. ''bewrecan'', exile, send forth: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wreak.'']   To avenge; revenge.
{{smaller block|Thus much am I ''bewreke.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Wife of Bath’s Tale (ed. Speght), l. 809.}}}}

'''bewreck†''' (bẹ̄-rek′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''wreck.'' Cf. AS. ''bewrecan'', drive or bring to, of ships: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''wreck.'']   To ruin; destroy.
{{smaller block|Yet was I, or I parted thence, ''bewreckt.''
{{right|''Mir. for Mags.''}}}}

'''bewrought†''' (bẹ̄-rôt′). Obsolete past participle of ''bework.''

'''bey'''<sup>1</sup> (bā), ''n.''   [= F. Sp. ''bey'', < Turk. ''bey'', ''beg'' = Pers. ''baig'', a lord: see ''beg''<sup>2</sup>, ''beglerbeg'', and ''begum''.]   '''1.''' The governor of a minor province or sanjak of the Turkish empire.—'''2.''' A title of respect given in Turkey to members of princely families, sons of pashas, military officers above the rank of major, the wealthy gentry, and, by courtesy, to eminent foreigners.
{{smaller block|We therefore rode out of Beyrout as a pair of Syrian ''Beys''.
{{right|''B. Taylor'', Lands of the Saracen, p. 33.}}}}
'''3.''' The title usually given by foreigners to the former Mohammedan rulers of Tunis.

Frequently written ''beg''.

'''bey'''<sup>2</sup>†, ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''buy''.

'''beyete'''†, ''v. t.'' A Middle English form of ''beget''.

'''beylerbey''' (bā′lėr-bā′), ''n.''   [< Turk. ''beylerbey'', ''beglerbeg'', prince of princes, lit. ‘bey of beys.’]   The title of the governor-general of a province of the Turkish empire, ranking next to the grand vizir, and so called because he has under him the ''beys'' at the head of the several sanjaks or districts composing his province. Also written ''beglerbeg.''

'''beylerbeylik''' (bā′lėr-bā′lik), ''n.''   [Turk., < ''beylerbey'' + ''-lik,'' a common noun formative; cf. ''beylik.'']   The territory governed by a beylerbey. Also ''beglerbeglik'' or ''beglerbeglic.''

'''beylik''' (bā′lik), ''n.''   [Turk., < ''bey,'' a bey, + ''-lik;'' cf. ''beylerbeylik.'']   The district ruled by a bey.

'''beyond''' (bẹ̄-yond′), ''prep.'' and ''adv.''   [< ME. ''beyonde, beyende,'' etc., < AS. ''begeondan,'' < ''be,'' by, + ''geondan,'' from the further side, < ''geond,'' prep., across, over, beyond (= Goth. ''jāins,'' yonder), + ''-an,'' adv. suffix: see ''be-''<sup>2</sup> and ''yon, yonder.'']   '''I.''' ''prep.'' '''1.''' On or to the other side of: as, ''beyond'' the river; ''beyond'' the horizon; “''beyond'' that flaming hill,” ''G. Fletcher,'' Christ’s Victory and Triumph.
{{smaller block|We send our best commodities ''beyond'' the seas.
{{right|''Burton,'' Anat. of Mel., To the Reader, p. 59.}}}}
'''2.''' Further on than; more distant than: as, a mile ''beyond'' the river; a hundred miles ''beyond'' Omaha; he never could get ''beyond'' simple equations.
{{smaller block|<poem>So far your knowledge all their power transcends,
As what should be ''beyond'' what is extends.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden,'' Prol. to Univ. of Oxford, l. 39.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is not necessary to look ''beyond'' Nature or ''beyond'' experience in order to find that unique Object of which theology speaks. {{right|''J. R. Seeley,'' Nat. Religion, p. 52.}}}}
'''3.''' Past in time; later than: as, a day ''beyond'' the proper time.—'''4.''' At a place or time not yet reached by; before; ahead or in advance of.
{{smaller block|<poem>What’s fame? A fancied life in others’ breath; A thing ''beyond'' us, even before our death.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, iv. 238.}}}}
'''5.''' Out of reach of; outside of the capacity, limits, or sphere of; past: as, ''beyond'' our power; ''beyond'' comprehension; that is ''beyond'' me.
{{smaller block|We bring a welcome to the highest lessons of religion and of poetry out of all proportion ''beyond'' our skill to teach.
{{right|''Emerson'', Success.}}}}
{{smaller block|That the Antarctic continent has a flat and even surface, the character of the icebergs shows ''beyond'' dispute.
{{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Cosmology, p. 74.}}}}
'''6.''' Above; superior to; in or to a degree which rivals, exceeds, or surpasses, as in dignity, excellence, or quality of any kind.
{{smaller block|''Beyond'' any of the great men of my country.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}
{{smaller block|''Dangle.'' Egad, we were just speaking of your tragedy.—Admirable, Sir Fretful, admirable!

''Sneer.'' You never did anything ''beyond'' it, Sir Fretful—never in your life.
{{right|''Sheridan'', The Critic, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|She is beautiful ''beyond'' the race of women.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 113.}}}}
'''7.''' More than; in excess of; over and above.
{{smaller block|<poem>O, I’ve been vexed
And tortured with him ''beyond'' forty fevers.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|He [Pitt] refused to accept one farthing ''beyond'' the salary which the law had annexed to his office.
{{right|''Macaulay'', William Pitt.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Beyond all.''' See ''all.''—'''Beyond seas,''' out of the country; abroad.—'''To go beyond,''' to exceed in operation, ability, attainment, or the like; hence, in a bad sense, to deceive or circumvent.}}
{{smaller block|That no man ''go beyond'' and defraud his brother in any matter.
{{right|1 Thes. iv. 6.}}}}
<poem>The king has ''gone beyond'' me; all my glories
In that one woman I have lost for ever.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. VIII., iii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller|'''To go beyond one’s self,''' to be much excited by anything; be beside one’s self.   ''Nares.''}}

'''II.''' ''adv.'' At a distance; yonder.

{{smaller block|''Beyond'' he lyeth, languishing.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. i. 38.}}}}

'''beyond''' (bē-yond′), ''n.'' That place or state which lies on the other side; an experience or<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
